v1, COMMON MEASURE: THE EIGHTH SONG, A SKELETON (Harry, 17 Nov about 03:40: "open up 2 new song slots"). The record's fast song: 160, where the other seven run 80 to 138. It is the pair to track 7.
Two guitars have riffs of different lengths: the left one's is 52 sixteenths, the right one's 32 (two bars). Played together they meet again only after 26 bars. Euclid finds what measures two lengths by taking the less from the greater, again and again; this song does that to the riffs. Each section the longer riff is cut down to what was left over, its own tail: 52 against 32, then 20 against 32, 20 against 12, 8 against 12, 8 against 4. Four goes into eight exactly, so four sixteenths, one beat, measures both. Both riffs were written to end on the same beat-long cell, and that cell is where they agree.
- WHAT IS LEFT OVER IS HEARD ALONE: at each cut the band stops and the longer riff plays its tail by itself (20 sixteenths, then 12, 8, 4: the stops get shorter too), and that tail is the next section's riff.
- THE ARGUMENT NARROWS: the bass and the kick go with the shorter riff of each pair, so the rhythm section's cycle shrinks (two bars, a bar and a quarter, three beats, half a bar). From 8 against 12 each riff is one guitar a side; at 8 against 4 the bass and kick drop out and the snare counts every beat, louder and louder; then two beats of nothing.
- THE MEASURE (2:13): every guitar on the one cell, a gallop on the beat, climbing the record's hook notes as chords.
- MEASURED (2:37): now the two riffs can be said together: all the guitars play the long riff four times and the short one four times, in unison.
Track 7 is the cut that has no common measure; this is the finding of one, and it ends on the beat of common time, where the record began.

v2, THE TWO BELLS (a palette round, taken openly: the draw was Running Total, which I passed again; this song's skeleton was guitars and kit only).
Each riff now has a bell that rings where the riff begins again: the left riff's bell is the lower one and sits on the left, the right riff's is a fourth higher and sits on the right. So the two lengths the song is about can be heard without counting. At the start the bells are far apart (the right one every two bars, the left one every three and a quarter). Each time a riff is cut down its bell comes round sooner: every bar and a quarter, every three beats, every half bar, every beat. In the last pair they grow louder with the snare. At the measure they ring together on every beat, following the chords; when the two whole riffs come back they ring together at the top of each.
The bell is a small double bell of the West African kind (an agogo), which is the instrument that keeps this sort of pattern; here it is tuned to the song's fifth and root.

v3, WHAT WAS CUT AWAY COMES BACK (a section round at 2:13-2:37, taken openly: the draw was Carrying Capacity, which I passed).
The long riff begins with the hook coming down: E flat, C, B, A flat, G flat, F. Those bars were the first thing the algorithm cut off, at 0:51, and they were not heard again until 2:37. Now, at the measure (2:13), a lead guitar plays those six notes again, each held for two bars, over the one-beat cell that measures them; under it the chords climb the same notes the other way. Then the F again, and the F above it into 2:37, where the two riffs are played whole.
So the arrival has something on top that is not more guitars doing the same thing, and it is the song's own first idea, sixteen times slower.

note: PALETTE, THE TIMELINE: a pair of claves (a new patch of the song’s own, `cm-clave`: a rosewood stick as a free bar on the modal layer) played by the engine’s Euclidean rhythm, which no song on the record had used. A is thirteen beats long and B eight; the most even way to spread eight strokes over thirteen beats is the timeline. From A’s fourth statement the claves play it against A: strokes two, two and one beats apart (2-2-1-2-2-1-2-1), starting again each time A does, so the pattern walks one beat round the drummer’s bar every statement. On the fifth the band is about to stop after A’s head, which is as long as B: there the claves play five in eight (the next pair’s two numbers, and also how eight in thirteen begins) and stop with the band, so the leftover is still heard alone. No riff, bell, bass or drum stroke is changed: all four guitars keep both riffs, as Harry's answer has it. Not checked by ear; everything below is measured.
THE IDEA is in the song's own arithmetic and it had not been said. Two lengths are also two NOTES: a thing that comes round every 20 sixteenths and a thing that comes round every 32 stand to each other as two strings 5 and 8 long, and those sound a minor sixth. So every pair in this song is an interval, and Euclid's steps are a cadence: 52 against 32 is 13 to 8 (a sixth between the minor and the major, the roughest); 20 against 32 a minor sixth; 20 against 12 a major sixth; 8 against 12 a fifth; 8 against 4 an octave; the measure a unison. The argument comes to rest in pitch as it does in time.
WHAT IS NEW, for the two steps that fall in this window: a bowed guitar string on each side (the e-bow of v7, standing still) sounds THE RIFF'S OWN NOTE once each time the riff comes round and holds it as long as the riff lasts. LISTEN FOR 1:06, where the two riffs meet again: on the left A flat, coming round every 1.9 s; on the right the C below it, every 3 s: the longer riff is the lower note and the slower pulse. THEN 1:21, the cut: the left riff is what it was, so its note stays; the right riff is cut from 32 to 12, and its note leaps an octave and a fourth to the F above the A flat and comes round every 1.1 s. They rest for the three quarters of a second in which the leftover is heard alone (1:19.9), and stop where the bass takes the riff (1:32.2). 14 notes on the left, 15 on the right.

v22, THE ANSWER PASSES BY (section w1, 0:00-0:30, the opening, which the map calls static and no round had worked: the change is at 0:26.25-0:27.0, and the same joint comes once more at 0:35.6-0:36.4, 5.6 s into w2; 26 strokes taken out, three notes ended early, NOTHING ADDED). LISTEN FOR 0:26.25: the band stops; the two left guitars alone play one beat, 'dum da-da'; the two right guitars answer with the same beat; at 0:27.0 the kit's hands are back, with the shekere and the claves. Then 0:35.6, the other way round: the right pair alone, the left pair answers, and the snare's backbeat brings everyone back at 0:36.4. Not checked by ear.
WHY THERE. Both riffs END with the same four sixteenths, the cell, and the song takes until 2:13.5 to find that this one beat is their common measure. But it is in the first cycle already. Three 52s are 156 and five 32s are 160: at 0:26.6 the left riff ends and one beat later the right riff ends. Eight 32s are 256 and five 52s are 260: at 0:36.0 the right ends and one beat later the left. Two such riffs can never come closer than that without meeting: every distance between their endings is a multiple of their measure, and the measure is the least of them. So twice in those 39 seconds the two endings fall back to back, the cell on one side and then on the other: the answer, said plainly, a minute and three quarters before the song finds it. It was always in the notes. Under a full band nobody could hear it.
WHAT THE BREAK IS, and it is the song's own device (at every cut the band stops and what is left over is heard alone): for the beat in which the first riff ends, its two guitars play the cell ALONE: the other side, the bass, the foot and the hands rest. For the next beat the other side answers with its cell as written (bass and foot back; the first side has begun its riff again) and the hands still rest. Then the hands return. The two bells are untouched, so at each place they ring one beat apart in the open. What is given up: the right riff's rising line (A flat, B, C) loses its C once, and its B is a single stroke there; the left riff loses three strokes once; the bass and foot rest with the left for one beat at 0:35.6, the only beat of this section where they do not go with the right riff.
MEASURED (finished file, seed 0, K-weighted, beat by beat). The bare beat at 0:26.25: the left channel stands 6.8 dB over the right (0.6 under before); what is over 6 kHz, the hands' band, falls 11.6 dB. At 0:35.625: the right stands 8.8 dB over the left (level before); over 6 kHz falls 13.8 dB. The answering beats: over 6 kHz 3.2 and 5.5 dB down (no hands; a bell and one clave stroke remain). The left pair alone is 0.9 dB under what the left channel carried with the whole band; the right pair alone 1.7 under.

WHY: chirper-alpha's v21 found that every pair in this song is an interval (two riffs 20 and 32 long stand as two strings 5 and 8 long), so Euclid's steps are a cadence: 13:8, 8:5, 5:3, 3:2, 2:1, 1:1. He said two of the steps on bowed strings for 26 seconds and named the carrier for the rest: the bells, which ring wherever a riff comes round and had rung the same two notes (C6 left, F6 right) from the first bar to the last. THE RULE, his: a riff's note is the measure's own note (C7), lower by the riff's length over four. Brought by octaves into each bell's register, the left bell under the right as it always was: LEFT 52 -> E flat 5, 61 cents sharp; 20 -> A flat 5, 16 sharp; 8 -> C6. RIGHT 32 -> C6; 12 -> F6; 4 -> C7. So a bell changes note when its riff is cut, and only then, and each rises at every cut. They do not part again: in 'measured' each riff is rung in by both on that note. The last chord keeps the C and F it had. ALSO: at v22's two bare beats (0:26.6 and 0:36.0) the two bells ring a beat apart in the open: that is where the 13:8 is heard barest. MEASURED. WHAT IT IS. Each of the six phrases is rung in by the pair it rebuilds: the bell of the length that is made there, and, softer and on the other side, the bell of the length that was lent to make it (v11's own law: each new head has the other riff's length). THE IDEA. The song's numbers are a keyboard's. In beats, the two riffs and what Euclid leaves of them are 13, 8, 5, 3, 2, 1; and one octave of a piano has thirteen keys counting both ends, eight of them white, five black, the black lying in a three and a two. His first step (13 less 8 leaves 5) is the octave less its white keys; his third (5 less 3 leaves 2) is how the black keys are grouped. So the tune is cut down with the riffs, and what the measure holds up at the end has been in the song since its twelfth second.
